verses.1: Al-Mizan notes that majd means abundant nobility and that the oath by the glorious Qur’an has an implicit answer indicated by what follows: the Resurrection is true, the Prophet is among the warners, or the warning is true. It rejects proposed explicit answers in later verses, including ‘Rather they consider it odd’ (50:2) and ‘We know what the earth diminishes from them’ (50:4), as unsupported and nonsensical.
verses.2: Al-Mizan explains bal as turning from the implicit answer to the oath: either the Prophet was truly sent as a warner or the Resurrection he warns of is real, but the people disbelieved and found this strange. ‘From among themselves’ may mean that they objected to a human prophet of their own species, or, more pointedly, to an Arab from their own people explaining truth in their language. Calling them faithless rather than polytheists shows that they covered a truth that had come to them—namely resurrection and return to God.
verses.3: Al-Mizan glosses rajʿ as rujūʿ, return, and baʿīd as far from good sense. The deniers leave unstated the consequence of death and becoming dust—whether they will be returned to life—because their rhetorical question treats the claim as too absurd even to say aloud. Their reply that it is a far-fetched return expresses astonishment at being revived after nothing appears to remain of them.
verses.4: Al-Mizan says that God answers resurrection scepticism by affirming complete knowledge of whatever the earth consumes from each decayed body; no particle escapes Him, so restoration poses no difficulty. Alternatively, the wording can mean that He knows who dies, is buried, and is gradually consumed. The preserving Book preserves all things, their effects and states, or records all events without alteration; it is the Guarded Tablet (lawḥ al-maḥfūẓ), not the Record of Deeds. The latter reading is rejected because the verse concerns what the earth takes from bodies, and the Qur’an calls the Guarded Tablet, not the record of deeds, preserving. Thus their claim that God cannot identify dispersed bodily parts is false.
verses.5: Al-Mizan glosses marīj as confusion and muddle. Although the preceding response could suggest that resurrection-scepticism results from ignorance of God’s all-encompassing knowledge and the Guarded Tablet, this verse identifies the deeper cause as obstinate denial of truth they plainly recognize. Their perplexity lies in seeing the truth yet refusing it, contrary to the ordinary connection between knowing and believing. It may also describe their inconsistent accusations—at times calling the message a lie about God, magic, poetry, soothsaying, or madness—which are then rebuked by signs of divine knowledge and power and followed by warning through destroyed earlier nations.
verses.6: Al-Mizan explains furūj as gaps or cracks. The heavens are called ‘above them’ because they are plainly visible, and their stars are their adornment. Their beautiful, flawless construction is presented as the clearest evidence of God’s boundless knowledge and absolute power.
verses.7: Al-Mizan takes spreading out the earth to mean making it expansive and suitable for human life. Rawāsī is the plural of ‘firm,’ with mountains implicit rather than stated in the Arabic; bahīj denotes what delights the beholder, and the verse means the growth of every kind of beautiful plant. These providential features of the earth are rational evidence of God’s perfect knowledge and power.
verses.8: Al-Mizan reads this as a purposive clause: God built the heavens, spread the earth, and filled it with signs of providence so that every servant who turns back to Him may gain insight from them and reflect on their admonition.
verses.9: Al-Mizan identifies the heaven here as what is high above, the salubrious water as rain rich in goodness, bāsiqāt as extremely tall palms, talʿ as their first appearing fruit, and naḍīd as layered spathes. Gardens, harvested grain, and palms are provision for servants, displaying the Creator’s infinite knowledge and power and thus answering the claim that dispersed bodies cannot be revived. The revival of dead land by rain supplies a second resurrection proof: restoring people from their graves after death is no different in possibility from restoring plants that had lost their power to grow and spread.

verses.12: Al-Mizan treats the nations named in (50:12–14) as a warning to polytheists who obstinately denied a truth that had become clear. Their denial of the messengers made God’s threatened destruction due, as the fate of earlier deniers shows. It identifies the inhabitants of Aykah as the people of Shuʿayb and refers readers to the commentary’s earlier discussions of Rass, Aykah, and Tubbaʿ.

verses.15: Al-Mizan explains ʿayy primarily as incapacity, so the rhetorical question denies that God was unable to originate the present natural order, including heaven, earth, and humanity; it rejects restricting the first creation to either heaven and earth alone or humanity alone. The new creation is the Hereafter’s second world, encompassing all three (14:48), whose enduring, deathless order differs from this transitory world: felicity has unmixed enjoyment and wretchedness unmixed pain. Though ʿayy can also mean tiredness, the incapacity reading is more eloquent because the polytheists alleged the Resurrection’s impossibility, not its difficulty. The point is that the One whose knowledge and power ordered the first world can recreate it; confusion (labs, iltibās) belongs to the doubting polytheists, not to God.
verses.16: Al-Mizan takes ‘We created man’ as the human being’s continuing, changing creation and dependence on divine generosity, not merely his original formation. Its past tense and the present clauses about what the soul whispers and God’s nearness together express realities continuous with a person’s existence: creation demonstrates power; knowing outward and hidden reality, even doubts of resurrection, demonstrates all-encompassing knowledge. Waswasah is ascribed to the nafs—not to Satan, though it may also be his act—to show that this knowledge reaches the soul’s deepest thoughts. ‘Nearer … than ḥabl al-warīd,’ the veins, especially the jugular, is an accessible comparison; in truth God mediates between the soul and itself, its powers and actions, and is nearer than everything, even its contents (8:24).
verses.17: Al-Mizan identifies the mutalaqqiyān, whose talaqqī is taking note, as the angels entrusted with recording a human being’s deeds. It prefers taking ‘when’ as an implicit injunction to mention their recording, a distinct demonstration of God’s knowledge through recorded acts alongside His unmediated knowledge, rather than joining it to ‘nearer’ in the preceding verse; it also rejects making the angels’ record the cause or explanation of God’s knowledge as unfitting Qur’anic style. Their right and left positions symbolize the two sides of good and evil, with each recording a kind of action. The next verse specifies speech after deeds generally: lafẓ is speech, and a raqīb ʿatīd is a watchful observer ready for his duty.

verses.19: Al-Mizan explains sakrah of death as the soul’s wrenching away, which so isolates a person in self-concern that he resembles an intoxicated person. Death ‘brings the truth’ because it belongs to al-qaḍāʾ al-ilāhī and necessarily serves the cosmic order: as a passage from one abode to another, it is true, as are resurrection, paradise, and hell (21:35). What one had shunned—ḥīd, turning away or fleeing—thus arrives; natural aversion to death arises from worldly adornment and attachment, which God made a test (18:8).
verses.20: Al-Mizan treats the trumpet as the second journey to everlasting life after death: the first blast brings all things to an end and the second begins the Hour, and the verse may mean the second or both together. The threatened day is the Resurrection, when God carries out His warning of punishment to sinful servants.
verses.21: Al-Mizan defines the sāʾiq as a driver who urges cattle from behind, unlike a qāʾid who leads from the front. Each soul will stand before God for judgment with such a driver and a witness to its deeds. The verse does not expressly identify them as angels or as the recorders, though its preceding context suggests angels and the commentary defers the relevant narrations; it also does not limit the Day’s witnesses to this one.
verses.22: Al-Mizan reads the rebuke as addressed on Resurrection Day to every human being, though its tone may particularly concern deniers of the Resurrection. In this world people relied on apparent means and were thereby wholly enclosed in unawareness (ghāfil) of the reality that all means fail and return is to the Almighty; then God removes the veil and the heart’s sight directly perceives it. The verse therefore teaches both that the Day lifts ignorance so realities appear as they are and that what is then witnessed already exists while people are in the world, hidden rather than absent. The commentary rejects the claim that it addresses the Prophet before his mission, since neither context nor wording supports it.
verses.23: Al-Mizan says the tone suggests that the companion is the angel appointed over the person. If it is the driver, ‘what is ready with me’ means the human being present with him; if the witness, it means the person’s deeds ready for testimony. It reports the alternative that the companion is a devil, in which case he says the person whose affairs he controlled is ready for hell.
verses.24: Al-Mizan takes the command to cast into hell as describing connected traits: the kaffār, intensely unbelieving or ungrateful; the ʿanīd, obstinately opposed to truth; the hinderer of good; the mutaʿaddī, who oversteps truth and the bounds of ʿubūdiyyah into arrogance and rebellion; and the murīb, who either doubts or creates doubt about Resurrection. Extreme rejection breeds obstinacy, the obstruction of good, transgression, and doubt. God appears to address the driver and witness, although it may instead be two custodians of hell.

verses.26: Al-Mizan explains that the verse expansively says ‘who has set up another god’ rather than briefly calling him a mushrik, to emphasize shirk as the gravest sin and the source of the preceding faithlessness, obstinacy, hindering of good, transgression, and scepticism. Repeating the command to cast him in intensifies it: idolatry makes the punishment more severe.
verses.27: Al-Mizan identifies the companion definitively as the devil assigned to each person, the Qur’anic companion who whispers and seeks to mislead (43:36–38). Before God, the devil acknowledges His lordship and says he did not compel the person’s rebellion; the person freely accepted his promptings while already in extreme error, so the devil disclaims responsibility for those sins.
verses.28: Al-Mizan takes God to be addressing rebellious idolaters and their companions collectively before the address narrows to each person and companion. ‘Do not wrangle’ means that disputing before Him cannot benefit them, because He had already delivered the warning to those who associate partners with Him and do wrong. The warning is exemplified by His words to Iblīs and his followers (17:63) and by the decree to fill hell with guilty jinn and humans (32:13).
verses.29: Al-Mizan treats the verse as independent of the previous one and as answering whether the prior warning might be changed or waived. ‘The word’ (al-qawl) is God’s definitive decree that whoever dies in disbelief enters hell, the warning given to Iblīs and his followers; ‘with Me’ qualifies its unalterability. His punishment is not injustice, since warning preceded it, no excuse remains, and servants are requited only with deeds they sent ahead (66:7). Ẓallām negates tyrannical injustice without implying that lesser injustice is possible: any injustice in recompense for the many wrongdoers would itself be enormous by quantity.
verses.30: Al-Mizan rejects both the view that the exchange is al-khiṭāb wa al-jawāb bi lisān al-ḥāl, an allegory of the situation, and the view that it is really between God and hell’s custodians: the first would not explain why God alone addresses hell, and the second departs from the apparent wording without evidence. It accepts the apparent real exchange, since God can make hands, feet, skin, and other seemingly inanimate beings speak, and all beings have some degree of awareness. Both questions are rhetorical and perhaps show that divine might and punishment fully encompass the wrongdoers (9:49). The exchange may occur before hell is fully populated, answering the apparent tension with (38:85); alternatively, ‘Is there any more?’ implies ‘No more,’ affirming that it is full and perhaps alluding to (32:13), a reading supported if the prior unalterable word is that decree.
verses.31: Al-Mizan explains that on the Resurrection Day paradise will be brought directly before the Godwary, in a place not far from them, so they enter it without difficulty. Uzlifat means brought near, while ghayr baʿīd describes their proximity.
verses.32: Al-Mizan identifies the promised reward as belonging to every awwāb, one who continually returns to God through repentance and obedience, and every ḥafīẓ, one who constantly observes the prohibitions God has imposed.
verses.33: Al-Mizan explains this as a bayān of the penitent and dutiful person: fearing the All-beneficent bi al-ghayb is fearing His hidden, unseen punishment, while a qalb munīb is a heart formed by a lifetime of returning to God through inābah.
verses.34: Al-Mizan says the Godwary are told to enter paradise in peace: either sound and secure from all evil and harm, or receiving peace invoked by God and His angels. ‘The day of immortality’ is their glad tiding.
verses.35: Al-Mizan prefers connecting fīhā (‘in it’) to ‘they wish,’ because that reading best accords with God’s boundlessness: paradise’s inhabitants have every conceivable object or end they might desire, without limit or exception. ‘With Us there is yet more’ must therefore name a perfection beyond what they can conceive or desire. It rejects the narrowing claims that this means merely extra desired provision—whether in the reported cloud story—or tenfold multiplication of deeds, since the first clause already grants every possible desire.
verses.36: Al-Mizan says this threat follows the preceding argument for Resurrection, as elsewhere in the sūrah an argument is followed by warning. God destroyed many generations before the contemporary idolaters though they were stronger, ravaged lands, conquered towns, and ruled them; none could find refuge from His punishment and destruction.
verses.37: Al-Mizan defines the qalb as the faculty by which one distinguishes truth from falsehood, good from evil, and benefit from harm; without reflection and use of it, it is as though one has no heart. To ‘give ear’ (ilqāʾ al-samʿ) is to listen, and shahīd means being present and attentive, not merely physically but in comprehension. The account and ruined nations admonish either the person able to discern and acknowledge truth independently or the one unable to do so who listens to and follows true speech. One who does neither is a wilfully ignorant jāhil mutaʿannit, like those who say, ‘Had we listened or applied reason…’ (67:10).
verses.38: Al-Mizan glosses lughūb as toil and reads the verse as the clear denial that any fatigue touched God in creating the heavens, earth, and all between them in six days.
verses.39: Al-Mizan explains that the command to be patient follows the sūrah's warnings to deniers of the Resurrection. Tasbīḥ is declaring God free of what they ascribe to Him while praising Him (ḥamd), thus affirming His beautiful acts and denying every deficiency. The times before sunrise and sunset may denote ṣalāt al-subḥ and ṣalāt al-ʿaṣr, or also ṣalāt al-ẓuhr; part of the night may denote maghrib and ʿīshāʾ. Adbār al-sujūd means after prayer, and may refer to taʿqībāt al-ṣalāt, nawāfil after the farāʾiḍ, post-sunset rakʿah, or the end-of-night witr.

verses.41: Al-Mizan takes istamiʿ here most aptly as intiẓār: the Prophet is to expect the day when the angel blows the trumpet. Its call comes from a makān qarīb because it encompasses all humanity, so every hearer is equally near to it; it is the Resurrection's call and word of life. The Cry is bi al-ḥaqq because it proceeds from God's definitive qaḍāʾ, and the verse is a bayān of that call: the dead rise from their graves and hasten forth, as in (70:43).

verses.43: Al-Mizan defines iḥyāʾ as giving bodies life in this world and imātah as causing the living to die and enter the world of the grave. In this context, the destination to God alludes to their being given life again at the Resurrection.
verses.44: Al-Mizan explains tashaqqaq as the earth cracking open around the dead, who emerge hastening toward the caller. The ease of mustering includes the earth's splitting, their swift emergence from the graves, and their gathering.
verses.45: Al-Mizan defines a jabbār as a dictator who compels people to do his will. The Prophet is therefore to endure their words, glorify his Lord, and await the Resurrection: God knows their speech and will recompense their deeds, while the Prophet has not been sent to force belief in God and the Last Day. He is to admonish with the Qur'an those who fear the threat.
